result.summary: This section gathers four short fragments attributed to the lost Precepts of Chiron, quoted by ancient writers. They give advice on sacrifice and fair judging, a riddle on the long lives of animals and Nymphs, and a note on whether Hesiod wrote the work.

scenes.title: Advice to honor the gods
scenes.summary: The speaker urges the listener to take these words to heart and to sacrifice to the gods on coming home.

scenes.title: Hear both sides
scenes.summary: A maxim tells the listener to judge no case until both parties have spoken.

scenes.title: Riddle of long life
scenes.summary: A ladder of lifespans runs from crow to stag, raven and phoenix, ending with the Nymphs who outlive them all.

scenes.title: Quintilian on authorship
scenes.summary: Quintilian notes a view on teaching young children, ascribed to Hesiod, and that Aristophanes rejected the Precepts as Hesiod's.

characters.name: Nymphs
characters.description: long-lived daughters of Zeus who outlive ten phoenixes

characters.name: Hesiod
characters.description: poet to whom the Precepts were attributed

characters.name: Aristophanes
characters.description: critic who rejected the Precepts as Hesiod's work

notable_quotes.reason: A lasting maxim of fair judgment: hear both sides before deciding.
A vivid riddle ranking animal lifespans up to the Nymphs.

analysis.text: The fragments show practical wisdom poetry: piety, fairness and reverence for the gods' order, in the manner of Hesiod's Works and Days.
The Precepts survive only in quotations, and ancient critics like Aristophanes doubted Hesiod wrote them.

legacy.text: The lifespan riddle of crow, stag, raven and phoenix was repeated by later writers, including Plutarch, and so survived.

fun_facts.text: The work is credited to the centaur Chiron, teacher of Achilles, who is imagined as instructing his pupil.

language_notes.text: The label cites a scholiast (ancient commentator) on Pindar's Pythian 6, which preserves this line; the Precepts survive only in quotations like this.
The lifespans multiply: crow nine generations, stag four times that, raven three times the stag, phoenix nine ravens, Nymphs ten phoenixes. Ancient sources treat a generation as a lifetime.
Aegis-holder is Zeus's epithet; the aegis was a divine goatskin shield or cloak that inspired terror.
Aristophanes here is the Alexandrian scholar Aristophanes of Byzantium, a critic of texts, not the comic playwright.

context_notes.text: Offering sacrifice to the gods on returning home reflects the Greek habit of honoring the gods at the hearth and household.
The Nymphs are female nature spirits, long-lived but not immortal in this riddle; the phoenix is a legendary bird said to live extremely long.
Quintilian was a Roman teacher of rhetoric; his Institutes of Oratory discuss when children should begin schooling.

literary_notes.text: The compounding multiplication of lifespans exaggerates age to a staggering scale, culminating in the Nymphs' near-endless life.
The riddle climbs step by step from crow to Nymphs, saving the speakers for last, so the self-reference lands as the peak.
